findings.summary: The label gate is `width >= 0.05 * top`, a fraction of the axis maximum rather than a test of whether the value fits its segment, so two segments wide enough to carry a number are drawn blank: at sixteen slices the factor segment is 104.9 ms and 56 px wide (the 105 would need about 27 px) and is unlabelled by 0.3 ms under the 5 percent cutoff, and at one slice the read-decision segment is 51.05 ms and 26 px wide and is unlabelled although '51' needs about 18 px. The brief asked for the value printed per stage where it fits. A reader must estimate both by position on the axis; factor is 5.6 percent of the sixteen-slice stage sum and is the third-largest stage.

findings.disposition_note: colour matching still resolves every stage and no reading of the figure is at stake; the stack and the key deliberately differ because the read stages are grouped by hue rather than by stack position.
findings.summary: The legend is placed with ncol=4 over seven handles, so matplotlib fills it column-major and it reads left-to-right as read census, read geometry, step assembly, back-solve on the first row and read decision, step residual, factor on the second. That order is not the stack order of the bars (census, decision, geometry, residual, assembly, factor, back-solve), so a reader walking the bar with the legend has to hunt for each colour instead of tracking the key in sequence. The swatches themselves are unambiguous.

findings.summary: The bar end (1879 ms at sixteen slices) and the dashed whole-solve mark (602 ms) are different quantities by a factor of 3.12, and the image carries no wording that says so: the label reads only 'whole solve, 602 ms per iterate' while the bar reaches 1879 ms. A reader who takes the bar as the iterate's wall leaves with a wall three times too high. The page caption does reconcile them ('the bar's end is an upper bound on the work and the mark is the measurement it is checked against'), so the figure is not misleading in place, but the image alone does not close the gap.
